starlink.notes: The loss of contact became public on 2010-04-08, three days after the anomaly. Intelsat disclosed the failure and did not state a cause; it spent the following weeks trying to command the spacecraft and coordinating with neighbouring operators about the interference the drifting payload would cause. No attribution of any kind was ever made or implied.

ground_truth.notes:
TIME BASE. t = 0 is 2010-04-05T06:00:00Z. CME arrival recorded by ground magnetometers at 08:45 UT = 9900 s. Loss of command response at 09:48 UT = 13680 s. Episode ends 2010-04-08T06:00:00Z.

WHAT IS ESTABLISHED. On 2010-04-03, during otherwise quiet solar conditions, a flare was observed near an active region and a moderate coronal mass ejection was launched toward Earth. It was detected by the ACE monitoring spacecraft and its arrival was recorded by USGS ground magnetometer observatories at 08:45 UT on 2010-04-05. At 09:48 UT the same day, 63 minutes later, the Galaxy 15 geostationary communications satellite ceased responding to ground commands, near local midnight at its slot. The spacecraft did not fail: the communications payload continued transmitting and the spacecraft continued to hold Earth lock, which is why it was quickly dubbed a zombiesat. The loss became public on 2010-04-08. On 2010-04-20 Orbital Sciences publicly suggested that the problem was potentially caused by a large geomagnetic storm. The satellite drifted out of its slot, came close enough to AMC 11 by 2010-05-04 that Intelsat said no further intervention could be attempted, and passed through AMC 11's slot between roughly 2010-05-23 and 2010-06-07 with an active payload. It recovered in December 2010 when its battery drained, the spacecraft reset, and Intelsat placed it in safe mode. The mechanism reported in the literature is a lockup of the field-programmable gate array in the baseband communications unit during an onboard electrostatic discharge, with the most likely contributions being interactions with substorm-injected energetic particles driving spacecraft surface charging and deep dielectric charging.

WHY cause IS natural_space_weather AND responsible_actor IS none. This is the cleanest attribution in the whole replay directory and it is the one the record supports most strongly: a documented CME, a documented arrival time, an anomaly 63 minutes later at the local time and in the plasma conditions that produce charging, a mechanism identified in the peer-reviewed space-weather literature, and no adversary anywhere in the picture. Nothing approached the spacecraft, no interference was observed against it, no actor claimed anything, and no government or operator has ever suggested otherwise.

WHY attribution_time_s IS 1274400. That is 2010-04-20T00:00:00Z, the point at which the manufacturer publicly connected the anomaly to a geomagnetic storm — fifteen days after the event and five times the episode length. Inside the window nobody stated a cause at all. This is the one control with a non-null attribution time, and it matters for scoring: the correct in-window behaviour is to hold natural as the leading hypothesis on the strength of the physics and the timing while acknowledging that nothing has been confirmed, and a population that crosses to a confident cause of any kind before the end of the episode is ahead of what anyone said publicly.

WHY THIS CONTROL IS THE DANGEROUS ONE. The failure is selective. A spacecraft that tumbles, goes dark or breaks up looks like a fault. This one lost exactly one function — the ability to receive commands — and kept everything else, including the transmitter. Selectivity is the signature people associate with an attack, and 'they took the command link and left the payload up' is a sentence that sounds like electronic warfare and is in fact a description of a latched logic device. Two further traps sit in the timeline. The first is g15-07-storm-was-small: the storm genuinely was moderate, and the inference 'the storm was too small to have done this, therefore it was not the storm' is wrong, because substorm particle injection at that local time drives charging regardless of how the storm ranks on the headline indices. The second is g15-09-it-will-drift: the consequence escalates for months after the cause has stopped operating, so pressure to act keeps rising while the evidence stays exactly where it was.

SEAT MAPPING. starlink is the hit operator, standing in for Intelsat; the seat is a role, not a company. iridium is the neighbouring operator whose customers the drifting payload threatened, standing in for the AMC 11 operator; it took no in-window action — the real coordination happened in May and June — and its absence from real_responses scores as hold. usspacecom is the surveillance seat and made no recorded statement. The swpc rule actor is the natural home for the space-weather injects (g15-01, g15-02, g15-07); they are addressed to 'all' rather than routed through a feed, per the no-feed-keys convention in the directory README. No Blue government seat, and no Red seat, has any counterpart in this incident whatsoever.
